newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan to revise liquor taxes along WTO ruling.
newsitem.headline: Japan to revise liquor taxes along WTO ruling.

text.p: Japan has agreed to raise taxes on domestic liquor and lower those for whiskey in order to comply with a World Trade Organisation (WTO) ruling, government officials said on Tuesday.
The WTO, ruling on a complaint by the European Union, the United States and Canada, said in November that Japan taxes foreign spirits at levels higher than that for domestic liquor.

A Ministry of Finance (MOF) official said Britain has accepted the plan and the European Union is likely to accept it soon. Canada and the United States have yet to reply formally, but are expected to follow suit, he said.
EU officials were not immediately available for comment.

The basic outline for the revision by the ruling Liberal Democratic Party calls for whiskey taxes to be slashed by around 58 percent over a two-year period to 10,225 yen ($90) per degree of alcohol per kilolitre in October 1998, he said.

Taxes on domestic spirits known as "shochu", a potent colourless liquor made mainly from barley, will be raised by about 1.6 times from the current rate over a two-year period to 9,924 yen ($87) per degree of alcohol per kilolitre in October 1998.

Another type of shochu, which has flavour and is made mostly by smaller local breweries, will be raised by about 2.4 times from the current rate over a five-year period, to 9,924 yen ($87) per degree of alcohol per kilolitre in October 2001.
Taxes on spirits such as vodka will also be set at 9,924 yen ($87) per degree of alcohol per kilolitre in October 1997.
The plan also calls for the government to provide financial assistance to brewers and manufacturers who are expected to be hard hit by the tax increase, the official added.

"Our business is going to be hit very hard because of the tax revision. The tax increase will no doubt affect our sales, and we have to seriously work out a new strategy," said Kiyoshi Ishikawa, a spokesman for Takara Shuzo Co Ltd, a leading maker of shochu.
Sales of shochu account for 30 percent of the company's overall sales. A 1.8-litre bottle of shochu, for instance, will be raised by about 170 yen ($1.50) from the present price of 1,240 yen ($11).
He said the move will almost certainly reduce sales.

Japan carries out a review of its entire taxation system towards the end of the year and relevant legislation is submitted to parliament early the following year. This would take effect from the start of the fiscal year on April 1.
This year's tax review programme is expected to be outlined on Wednesday.
